overview:
Murtipujaka (Mūrtipūjaka, literally “image‑worshipper”) is the largest sub‑sect of the Śvetāmbara Jain tradition and, in many contexts, the default form of Śvetāmbara Jainism encountered in western India. The term designates those Jains who integrate the worship (pūjā) of images (mūrti) of the Jinas or Tīrthaṅkaras into their religious life, in contrast to the aniconic Śvetāmbara Sthānakavāsī and Terāpanthī sub‑sects, which emphasize internal, contemplative worship (bhāva‑pūjā) without temple images. In everyday usage, Murtipujaka Śvetāmbaras are also called Derāvāsī (“temple‑dweller”), Mandir‑mārgī (“follower of the temple path”), Pujerā (“worshippers”), or Chaityavāsī (“temple residents”), all of which highlight their close association with temples and ritual spaces.

Historically, the Murtipujaka identity crystallized in the context of reform movements that criticized image worship. In the fifteenth century, the lay intellectual Loṅkā Śāh, working in Gujarat as a copyist of Jain manuscripts, argued that the canonical scriptures did not prescribe temple construction or image worship and that such practices risked violating ahiṃsā (non‑violence) through building activity and material offerings. His critique inspired later aniconic movements, including the Lonka sect and, subsequently, the Sthānakavāsī and Terāpanthī traditions. In response, Murtipujaka teachers and mendicants defended image worship on two main grounds: first, that veneration of Jina images and temples is deeply rooted in Jain cosmology and narrative history; and second, that images serve as powerful aids for laypeople, helping them cultivate devotion, ethical discipline, and right faith (samyag‑darśana) while remaining within the constraints of household life.

Doctrinally, Murtipujaka Śvetāmbaras share the core Jain commitments to non‑violence (ahiṃsā), non‑possessiveness (aparigraha), many‑sidedness of truth (anekāntavāda), and the path of liberation structured through right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct. They accept the authority of the Śvetāmbara canonical scriptures and trace monastic lineages back to Sudharman, a chief disciple of Mahāvīra. Within this shared framework, their distinctive emphasis lies in the ritual and symbolic world of temples. Building temples (jina‑bhavana), installing images, sponsoring festivals, and undertaking pilgrimages are understood as prabhāvanā—acts that “illuminate” and glorify the Jain dharma, generate merit (puṇya), and support the community. Classical cosmological narratives describe eternal Jina images and temples in regions such as Nandiśvara‑dvīpa, worshipped by gods like Indra, and universal histories recount primordial kings such as Bharata installing images of Ṛṣabha and other Jinas. For Murtipujakas, these stories affirm that image worship is not a late innovation but an expression of the timeless reverence for the Jinas.

In practice, Murtipujaka life is organized around temples (derāsar, mandir) and domestic shrines. Laypeople perform pūjā to Jina images using water, flowers, rice, incense, lamps, and sometimes saffron or sandal paste, while reciting praise hymns (stavan), mantras, and canonical or liturgical texts. The images themselves are not regarded as gods who intervene in worldly affairs but as perfected beings whose presence inspires detachment, ethical discipline, and the aspiration for liberation. Temples also house images of attendant deities (yakṣa and yakṣī), who are understood as powerful but still worldly beings; their veneration is framed within a broader hierarchy that places the Jinas and the path of liberation at the center.

Murtipujaka mendicants (monks and nuns) wear white robes, in keeping with Śvetāmbara norms, and many use a mouth‑covering cloth (muhpaṭṭī) while speaking to reduce harm to airborne organisms. They typically reside in temple complexes or specially designated monastic residences (upāśraya), and they maintain strict rules of wandering, food collection, and non‑attachment. While monks and nuns do not themselves perform elaborate material pūjā—because direct handling of water, flowers, and other offerings can conflict with ascetic regulations—they play a crucial role in guiding lay ritual life through sermons, scriptural teaching, and supervision of temple communities. Modern scholarship has shown that Murtipujaka mendicancy is closely intertwined with lay society, with monastic orders (gaccha) such as the Tapa Gaccha, Kharatara Gaccha, and others mirroring social and regional networks and undergoing significant reforms in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

Geographically, Murtipujaka Śvetāmbaras are especially prominent in Gujarat and Rajasthan, though they are now found throughout India and in diaspora communities worldwide. Their temples range from small urban shrines to monumental pilgrimage sites such as Śatruñjaya, with hundreds of temples and shrines clustered on a single sacred hill. Architecturally and artistically, Murtipujaka temples are renowned for intricate stone carving, iconographic programs that narrate Jain cosmology and ethics, and ritual spaces designed to support both individual meditation and communal worship. In contemporary contexts, Murtipujaka communities continue to negotiate questions of reform, ritual simplification, gender roles, and global identity, while maintaining the central conviction that properly understood and carefully practiced image worship can coexist with—and even strengthen—the rigorous non‑violent and ascetic ideals of Jainism.

Beyond the Śvetāmbara context, the term “murtipujaka” is sometimes used more broadly in scholarship and community discourse to describe any Jain group, Śvetāmbara or Digambara, that incorporates image worship into its religious life. In this wider sense, it functions as a descriptive label rather than a formal sectarian name. However, in most Jain self‑descriptions, “Murtipujaka” specifically denotes the Śvetāmbara image‑worshipping majority, distinguished from the Sthānakavāsī and Terāpanthī sub‑sects, and embedded in a long history of temple‑centered devotion, cosmological imagination, and lay‑monastic collaboration.

primary_sources.title: Kalpa‑sūtra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu; Śvetāmbara canonical text
primary_sources.original_text: जिनाणं पूजा बहुमहत्ता, तेसिं चैत्थाणं कत्तव्वं।
primary_sources.transliteration: jināṇaṃ pūjā bahumahattā, tesiṃ caitthāṇaṃ kattavvaṃ.
primary_sources.translation: The worship of the Jinas is of great importance, and their sacred places are to be established.
primary_sources.notes: The Kalpa‑sūtra is a key Śvetāmbara canonical text recited especially during the Paryuṣaṇa festival. While its primary focus is on the lives of the Jinas and monastic regulations, traditional Murtipujaka exegesis reads its references to honoring the Jinas and their sacred places as supporting the legitimacy of temples and image worship. The exact wording and interpretation vary across manuscripts and commentarial traditions, and the line given here represents a commonly cited, paraphrastic formulation used in community discourse rather than a critical edition verse.

primary_sources.title: Āvaśyaka‑sūtra (with traditional commentaries)
primary_sources.author: Canonical text; major commentaries by Haribhadra, Malayagiri, and others
primary_sources.original_text: नमो अरिहंताणं, नमो सिद्धाणं, नमो आयरियाणं, नमो उवज्झायाणं, नमो लोए सव्वसाहूणं।
primary_sources.transliteration: namo arihaṃtāṇaṃ, namo siddhāṇaṃ, namo āyariyāṇaṃ, namo uvajjhāyāṇaṃ, namo loe savvasāhūṇaṃ.
primary_sources.translation: Homage to the Arhats, homage to the Siddhas, homage to the Ācāryas, homage to the Upādhyāyas, homage to all the Sādhus in the world.
primary_sources.notes: The Āvaśyaka‑sūtra is central to daily Jain practice and is recited by both mendicants and laypeople. In Murtipujaka settings, this liturgy is frequently performed in front of Jina images, and commentaries explain how verbal homage (namo) and mental contemplation are harmonized with the visual presence of the mūrti. The text itself does not prescribe image worship, but its use within temple ritual is a key example of how canonical recitation and mūrti‑pūjā are integrated in Murtipujaka practice.

primary_sources.title: Universal History passages on Bharata and Ṛṣabha
primary_sources.author: Various Jain universal history texts; Śvetāmbara narrative tradition
primary_sources.original_text: भरतो चक्रवर्ती सत्रुंजयगिरिं आरुह्य जिनप्रतिमां प्रतिष्ठापयामास।
primary_sources.transliteration: bharato cakravartī satruñjayagiriṃ āruhya jinapratimāṃ pratiṣṭhāpayāmāsa.
primary_sources.translation: Emperor Bharata ascended Mount Śatruñjaya and installed an image of the Jina.
primary_sources.notes: Jain universal histories narrate the deeds of great kings and Jinas across cosmic time. In Murtipujaka discourse, stories of Bharata installing Jina images on Śatruñjaya and other sites are frequently cited to demonstrate the antiquity and cosmic significance of image worship. The line given here is representative of this narrative motif; exact phrasing differs among texts and editions. These narratives belong to a traditional corpus (tier B–C) that supports the theological claim that mūrti‑pūjā is rooted in primordial acts of devotion rather than being a purely medieval innovation.

primary_sources.title: Cosmological descriptions of Nandiśvara‑dvīpa
primary_sources.author: Jain cosmological texts such as the Saṃgrahaṇī‑sūtra and later compendia
primary_sources.original_text: नन्दीश्वरद्वीपे द्विपञ्चाशत् जिनालयाः नित्यं देवैः पूज्यन्ते।
primary_sources.transliteration: nandīśvaradvīpe dvipañcāśat jinālayāḥ nityaṃ devaiḥ pūjyante.
primary_sources.translation: On Nandiśvara‑dvīpa there are fifty‑two temples of the Jinas, eternally worshipped by the gods.
primary_sources.notes: Cosmological texts describe Nandiśvara‑dvīpa as a sacred island in the middle world, inaccessible to humans but filled with eternal Jina temples. Murtipujaka teachers use these passages to argue that temple worship is woven into the very structure of the Jain universe. The wording here summarizes a common cosmological description; specific verses vary by text and recension. These sources are important for the Murtipujaka claim that image worship has a cosmic, not merely historical, foundation.

misconceptions.myth: Murtipujaka Jains worship idols as gods who grant worldly boons, similar to popular Hindu deity worship.
misconceptions.reality: Murtipujaka Jains direct their worship primarily to the Jinas—perfected beings who have transcended the world and do not intervene in worldly affairs. The images are revered as symbolic and pedagogical representations of liberation, used to cultivate detachment, ethical discipline, and right faith. While attendant deities (yakṣa and yakṣī) may be acknowledged, the doctrinal focus remains firmly on the path to liberation rather than on seeking material favors.

misconceptions.myth: Image worship is a late, un‑Jain innovation that contradicts the original teachings of Mahāvīra and the canonical scriptures.
misconceptions.reality: Critics such as Loṅkā Śāh argued that the scriptures do not prescribe temples or images, but Murtipujaka traditions respond by pointing to cosmological descriptions of eternal Jina temples, universal history narratives of kings installing images, and long‑standing archaeological and textual evidence of early Jina images and shrines. For Murtipujakas, image worship is understood as a legitimate, scripturally compatible expression of reverence for the Jinas, especially suited to lay practice, when performed with awareness of non‑violence and non‑attachment.

misconceptions.myth: All Jains are Murtipujaka, and Jainism as a whole is simply an image‑worshipping religion.
misconceptions.reality: Jainism includes both image‑worshipping and aniconic traditions. Within the Śvetāmbara community, Murtipujakas are distinguished from Sthānakavāsī and Terāpanthī Jains, who reject temple images and emphasize internal, contemplative worship. Among Digambaras, there are also variations in the role of images. The term “Murtipujaka” therefore refers to specific image‑worshipping groups, not to all Jains, and Jain identity cannot be reduced to a single ritual style.

misconceptions.myth: Murtipujaka monks and nuns personally perform elaborate material pūjā rituals on the images.
misconceptions.reality: Murtipujaka mendicants follow strict ascetic rules that limit their direct involvement with material offerings such as water, flowers, and incense. Laypeople typically perform the pūjā rituals, while monks and nuns focus on scriptural teaching, ethical guidance, and supervision of community life. Mendicants may participate through recitation, presence, and instruction, but their primary role is to embody and transmit the ascetic and doctrinal ideals that give meaning to lay image worship.
